entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2026-0388: Pingora HTTP/2 :authority and Host header mismatch enables cache poisoning and host-based access control bypass
entry.content:
Pingora HTTP/2 :authority and Host header mismatch enables cache poisoning and host-based access control bypass

Aliases: CVE-2026-105298, GHSA-mgg9-6xw2-jfgp

Severity: CVSS_V4: CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N

Affected:

  • pingora-core — fixed in 0.9.0

Pingora versions prior to 0.9.0 accepted HTTP/2 requests whose Host header differed from the `:authority` pseudo-header. Request filters, cache keys, and logs that read the request URI (`session.req_header().uri`) saw the `:authority` value, but the upstream received the client-supplied Host value. Pingora also accepted `:authority` values containing userinfo (for example, `user@example.com`). This violates RFC 9113 Section 8.3.1, which requires an intermediary to use the `:authority` value for Host and replace any existing Host field. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a single HTTP/2 request that the application sees as one host and the upstream receives as another. Where request filters, access controls, or cache keys use the URI authority and the upstream routes by Host, this…

entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2026-0390: Pingora forwards client-nominated Connection headers to HTTP/1 upstreams, allowing ACL bypass in specific chained deployments
entry.content:
Pingora forwards client-nominated Connection headers to HTTP/1 upstreams, allowing ACL bypass in specific chained deployments

Aliases: CVE-2026-105299, GHSA-vx4q-2c55-cvmg

Severity: CVSS_V4: CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:N/SC:H/SI:H/SA:N

Affected:

  • pingora-proxy — fixed in 0.9.0

Pingora versions prior to 0.9.0 passed the downstream request through `upstream_request_filter` and wrote it to HTTP/1 upstreams without removing the client's Connection header, other hop-by-hop headers, or the headers Connection nominated, although RFC 9110 Section 7.6.1 requires intermediaries to remove them. The HTTP/2 upstream path already removed Connection and related HTTP/1-specific headers. A client could therefore nominate a header that the application adds in `upstream_request_filter` (for example, `Connection: keep-alive, X-Forwarded-For`). A downstream HTTP/1 intermediary that honors Connection would then strip the Pingora-added header before it reached the origin. This specifically affects chained deployments where an HTTP/1 intermediary between Pingora and the origin process…

entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2026-0389: Pingora HTTP/2 server memory exhaustion through unbounded default header-list and concurrent-stream limits
entry.content:
Pingora HTTP/2 server memory exhaustion through unbounded default header-list and concurrent-stream limits

Aliases: CVE-2026-105297, GHSA-7gpj-mj4q-x62x

Severity: CVSS_V4: CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N

Affected:

  • pingora-core — fixed in 0.8.1

Pingora versions prior to 0.8.1 used the h2 crate's default HTTP/2 server limits, a 16 MiB decoded header-list size and no limit on concurrent streams, unless the application set its own. A remote, unauthenticated client can send 1-byte HPACK references to a near-empty header, making the server allocate hundreds of thousands of header fields per stream across an unlimited number of streams on one connection, and use HTTP/2 flow control to keep those streams open. This can exhaust memory and degrade or terminate the Pingora process. This affects any Pingora service that terminates HTTP/2 (h2 or h2c) without explicitly setting `max_header_list_size` and `max_concurrent_streams`. The reporter showed that a single connection could get a Pingora process with a 2 GiB memory limit OOM-killed. T…

entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2026-0384: Race condition in `tokio::time::Interval` on Tokio v1.54.0
entry.content:
Race condition in `tokio::time::Interval` on Tokio v1.54.0

Aliases: CVE-2026-115567, GHSA-5wjr-9356-4wc8

Affected:

  • tokio — fixed in 1.54.1

## Summary On the multi-threaded runtime, there is a race condition between `Interval::poll_tick` and the runtime's time driver. This affects `Interval` only. `Sleep` and `Timeout` are **not** affected. ## Details In Tokio v1.54.0, a race condition between `tokio::time::Interval::poll_tick` (including `.tick().await`) and the runtime time driver can drop an internal timer entry without synchronizing with the driver thread that is firing it. This causes a data race and use-after-free on the timer's waker and task state in safe Rust, leading to assertion panics, task reference-count corruption, or heap memory corruption. This bug was introduced by https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/pull/8458, and it was fixed by https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/pull/8692. ## Impact This may lead to cr…
